## Groups {#sec-groups-def}

The definition, the first examples ($\Z/n$, $S_n$, $D_n$, $\GL(n,\C)$ and its
subgroups), homomorphisms and isomorphisms. See for now
[What a group is, and what it is for](https://neilshahcosmos.com/algebra/what-is-a-group.html).

## Subgroups, cosets and quotients {#sec-quotients}

Lagrange's theorem, normal subgroups, the quotient group $G/N$, and the first
isomorphism theorem: a homomorphism $\varphi : G \to H$ induces
$G / \ker\varphi \iso \im\varphi$. The running example is
$\SU(2) / \set{\pm I} \iso \SO(3)$.

## Representations {#sec-representations}

::: {#def-representation}
## Representation

A **representation** of a group $G$ on a vector space $V$ is a homomorphism
$\rho : G \to \GL(V)$. The dimension of $V$ is the dimension of the
representation. A representation is **unitary** if $V$ carries an inner product
and each $\rho(g)$ is unitary.
:::

Equivalence of representations, direct sums, the trivial representation, and
the regular representation on $\C[G]$.

## Complete reducibility {#sec-complete-reducibility}

A subspace $W \subseteq V$ is **invariant** if $\rho(g)W \subseteq W$ for all
$g$; a representation is **irreducible** if it has no invariant subspaces
other than $0$ and $V$.

::: {#thm-maschke}
## Maschke

Every finite-dimensional representation of a finite group over $\C$ is a direct
sum of irreducible representations.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Sketch.* Average any inner product over the group,
$\inner{v}{w}_G \defeq \frac{1}{\abs{G}} \sum_{g \in G} \inner{\rho(g)v}{\rho(g)w}$,
to obtain one for which $\rho$ is unitary. Then apply
@prp-invariant-complement repeatedly.
:::

The same averaging argument, with the sum replaced by an invariant integral
(Haar measure), is what makes the representation theory of *compact* Lie
groups such as $\SU(2)$ behave like that of finite groups. It fails for
non-compact groups such as the Lorentz group, which is why the
finite-dimensional spinor representations of $\SL(2,\C)$ are not unitary and
why Wigner's classification has to work with infinite-dimensional ones.

## Schur's lemma {#sec-schur}

::: {#lem-schur}
## Schur

Let $V$ and $W$ be irreducible representations of $G$ over $\C$, and
$T : V \to W$ a linear map commuting with the action of $G$. Then either
$T = 0$ or $T$ is an isomorphism; and if $V = W$, then $T = \lambda\, \id_V$
for some $\lambda \in \C$.
:::

::: {.proof}
$\ker T$ and $\im T$ are invariant subspaces, so each is $0$ or everything;
this gives the first statement. For the second, let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue
of $T$ (this is where $\C$ is used); then $T - \lambda\,\id$ commutes with $G$
and has nontrivial kernel, so it is zero.
:::

Schur's lemma is the reason a Casimir operator — an operator built from the
generators that commutes with all of them — acts as a scalar on each irreducible
representation, and therefore can be used to *label* irreducibles. Mass and
spin, in @sec-wigner, are exactly such labels.

## Characters {#sec-characters}

The character $\chi_\rho(g) = \Tr \rho(g)$, class functions, the orthogonality
relations, character tables for $S_3$ and $D_4$, and the decomposition of a
representation by taking inner products of characters.

## Looking ahead {#sec-wigner}

Everything in this chapter is finite-dimensional and about finite groups. The
next chapters replace "finite group" with "Lie group," at which point
representations become differentiable, the Lie algebra enters, and the
machinery above survives almost intact for compact groups. The payoff is
Wigner's theorem that particles are irreducible unitary representations of the
Poincaré group, previewed in
[the notes](https://neilshahcosmos.com/qft/wigner-classification.html).
